# Meniere disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Head and neck surgery > Meniere disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/gi0FIf)

---

## Summary

Meniere disease (<u>endolymph hydrops</u>) is a disorder of the <u>inner ear</u> caused by impaired endolymph resorption. The exact etiology of endolymph <u>malabsorption</u> is unknown but viral infections, <u>autoimmunity</u>, and <u>allergies</u> are thought to play a role. Meniere disease most commonly manifests in adults between 40–50 years of age. Clinical manifestations include recurrent episodes of <u>peripheral vertigo</u>, fluctuating unilateral <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u> (<u>SNHL</u>), and unilateral <u>tinnitus</u> (referred to as the <u>Meniere triad</u>); <u>horizontal nystagmus</u> or horizontal rotatory <u>nystagmus</u> may also be present. The episodes fluctuate in severity, typically lasting from 20 minutes to 12 hours. The diagnosis is based on characteristic clinical features and low to mid-frequency <u>SNHL</u> on <u>audiometry</u>. Treatment is symptomatic. <u>Vestibular suppressants</u> (e.g., <u>benzodiazepines</u> and <u>first-generation antihistamines</u>) may be used during acute <u>vertigo</u> attacks. Lifestyle modifications (e.g., avoidance of <u>allergens</u>, low-<u>sodium</u> diet) and <u>vestibular rehabilitation therapy</u> can help minimize the risk of recurrence. <u>Diuretics</u> should be considered in patients with frequent attacks. Interventional therapy (e.g., chemical vestibular <u>ablation</u> with intratympanic <u>gentamicin</u>, intratympanic <u>steroids</u>) or surgical vestibular <u>ablation</u> (e.g., <u>labyrinthectomy</u>, <u>vestibular neurectomy</u>) is reserved for patients with intractable symptoms that significantly impact their quality of life.




See also “<u>Vertigo</u>.”

## Epidemiology

* Sex: <u>♀</u> ≥ <u>♂</u> [[1]](/library/nPb72F)

* Onset: 20–60 years of age

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: : 40–50 years

* <u>Prevalence</u>: : 50–200 in 100,000 individuals in the US




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Pathophysiology

All patients with Meniere disease have impaired endolymph resorption that results in <u>endolymph hydrops</u>. However, not all patients with <u>endolymphatic hydrops</u> have symptoms of Meniere disease. The cause of impaired resorption is unknown. There are currently two main theories about why some patients develop symptoms:




* Endolymph hydrops: accumulation of fluid in the endolymphatic sac.

* Rupture theory: fluid accumulation in the endolymphatic sac → tear in the Reissner membrane  → increased perilymphatic <u>potassium</u> → <u>depolarization</u> of the afferent acoustic nerve fibers → symptom onset

* Compression theory: impaired endolymph resorption → compression of the <u>semicircular canals</u>  → symptom onset





> [!NOTE]
> The endolymph is rich in <u>potassium</u> and <u>perilymph</u> is rich in <u>sodium</u>. In Meniere disease, the concentration of <u>potassium</u> in the <u>perilymph</u> increases.

---

## Clinical features

Meniere disease characteristically manifests as recurrent episodes of acute, unilateral symptoms that last from minutes to hours. [[1]](/library/nPb72F)




### Meniere triad [[1]](/library/nPb72F)




* Peripheral <u>vertigo</u>

* <u>Tinnitus</u>

* Asymmetric fluctuating sensorineural <u>hearing loss</u> (<u>SNHL</u>)

* Low to mid-frequency <u>hearing loss</u> that progressively worsens with each episode

* May progress to <u>deafness</u> over several years

* <u>Tuning fork tests</u>  [[3]](/library/FIbgeE)

* <u>Weber test</u>: lateralization to the healthy <u>ear</u>

* <u>Rinne test</u>: bilaterally positive










### Additional symptoms




* Spontaneous horizontal or horizontal rotatory <u>nystagmus</u> [[4]](/library/_Pb5hF)[[5]](/library/xlbE_F)[[6]](/library/8ObO8F)

* Seen in some patients during an acute episode of Meniere disease

* The direction of <u>nystagmus</u> is variable and can change . [[5]](/library/xlbE_F)

* Can be supressed by visual fixation [[7]](/library/dmboe8)

* <u>Nausea and vomiting</u>

* <u>Ear</u> fullness





### Triggers



* Definitive triggers of Meniere disease are not known to exist  [[8]](/library/tObX8F)




### Progression




* Episodes fluctuate in severity and typically last from 20 minutes to 12 hours

* Periods of remission between attacks vary from months to years.

* In 10–25% of patients, the disease becomes bilateral.  [[1]](/library/nPb72F)

---

## Diagnosis

Meniere disease is diagnosed based on the characteristic clinical features and demonstrable low- to mid-frequency <u>SNHL</u> on <u>audiometry</u>. Specialized tests (e.g., <u>vestibular function testing</u>, <u>electrocochleography</u>) are reserved for patients with atypical symptoms or before attempting <u>ablative therapies</u>. <u>Neuroimaging</u> should be considered if <u>central vertigo</u> is suspected. See also “<u>Approach to vertigo</u>” for patients with undifferentiated <u>acute vestibular syndrome</u>. [[1]](/library/nPb72F)




### Diagnostic criteria for Meniere disease [[1]](/library/nPb72F)




* Definite Meniere disease: must include all of the following criteria

* ≥ 2 spontaneous attacks of <u>vertigo</u>, each lasting 20 min to 12 hrs

* Low to mid-frequency <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u> in the affected <u>ear</u> on <u>audiometry</u>

* Fluctuating aural symptoms in the affected <u>ear</u> (<u>hearing loss</u>, <u>tinnitus</u>, or <u>ear</u> fullness)

* Other suspected <u>causes of vertigo</u> excluded

* Probable Meniere disease: Patients that meet all of the above criteria but do not demonstrable <u>hearing loss</u> on <u>audiometry</u>.





### <u>Subjective audiometry</u> [[1]](/library/nPb72F)




* Indications

* All patients with suspected Meniere disease

* Before and after <u>ablative therapy</u>

* Modalities and characteristic findings: <u>Subjective audiometry</u> should always be performed in both <u>ears</u>. 

* Pure-tone <u>audiometry</u>: low- to mid-frequency <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u> (<u>SNHL</u>), with > 15 dB difference between the two <u>ears</u>

* <u>Speech audiometry</u> (with <u>word recognition score</u>): a difference of > 15% in <u>word recognition score</u> between the two <u>ears</u>





> [!TIP]
> Asymmetric fluctuating <u>hearing loss</u> is a characteristic feature of Meniere disease. <u>Subjective audiometry</u> may be normal at the time of testing because the attacks of Meniere disease are episodic. [[1]](/library/nPb72F)




![Audiogram in Meniere disease](media/og4fw0xt9si7sbfjm46okb6i.jpg)

Audiogram in Meniere disease




### Additional evaluation




#### <u>Vestibular function tests</u> and electrophysiologic testing [[1]](/library/nPb72F)




Not routinely recommended




* Indications

* Atypical symptoms

* Identifying the affected <u>ear</u>

* Before vestibular ablative procedures.

* Modalities and supportive findings

* <u>Vestibular function tests</u>: decreased vestibular function in the affected <u>ear</u>  [[9]](/library/YkbnmF)

* Electrocochleography: measures the summating potential (SP) generated by cochlear <u>hair</u> cells and the <u>action potential</u> (AP) of the cochlear nerve in response to acoustic stimulation
* Supportive findings: elevated SP/AP <u>ratio</u>

* Normal <u>vestibular function testing</u> or <u>electrocochleography</u> does not rule out Meniere disease.





#### Imaging [[1]](/library/nPb72F)[[10]](/library/QkbunF)




Imaging studies are not routinely indicated in patients with suspected Meniere disease.




* Indications

* To rule out differential diagnosis in patients with atypical symptoms (e.g., sudden <u>SNHL</u>, nonfluctuating <u>SNHL</u>)

* Before <u>ablative therapies</u>

* Preferred modality: <u>MRI</u> internal auditory canal and <u>posterior fossa</u> (without and with IV contrast)

* Supportive findings: endolymphatic space distention (<u>endolymphatic hydrops</u>) in the <u>cochlea</u> and vestibule  [[10]](/library/QkbunF)[[11]](/library/zlbrzF)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* See “<u>Causes of vertigo</u>” for other <u>etiologies of vertigo</u>.

* <u>Causes of peripheral vertigo</u>: e.g., meniere disease, <u>vestibular neuritis</u>

* <u>Causes of central vertigo</u>: e.g., <u>cerebellar stroke</u>, <u>vestibular migraine</u>, <u>multiple sclerosis</u>  [[13]](/library/wyahhM)

* See “<u>Differential diagnoses of vertigo</u>” for other conditions that mimic <u>vertigo</u>: e.g., <u>anxiety</u> or <u>panic disorder</u>, <u>postural hypotension</u>, medication side effects

* Traumatic <u>endolymphatic hydrops</u> (due to e.g., <u>head trauma</u>, <u>barotrauma</u>)

* <u>Otosclerosis</u>

* <u>Otosyphilis</u>  [[14]](/library/YNbn-F)[[15]](/library/bNbH-F)





> [!TIP]
> Always consider <u>vestibular migraine</u> as a differential diagnosis of Meniere disease.




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

There is currently no definitive cure for Meniere disease. Treatment is directed toward symptomatic management and prevention of recurrence. Interventional therapy or <u>surgery</u> is reserved for patients with intractable symptoms that significantly hinder their quality of life. [[1]](/library/nPb72F)




### Acute therapy [[1]](/library/nPb72F)




See “<u>Management of peripheral vertigo</u>” for more information and dosages.




* Consider short-term symptomatic pharmacotherapy with <u>vestibular suppressants</u> (e.g, <u>first-generation antihistamines</u>, <u>benzodiazepines</u>, <u>antiemetics</u>).

* Consider movement restriction.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Vestibular suppressants</u> are the treatment of choice for an acute <u>vertigo</u> attack in Meniere disease.




> [!WARNING]
> Chronic use of <u>vestibular suppressants</u> is contraindicated because of their potential to inhibit central compensation, which could elicit gait and <u>postural instability</u>.




### Recurrence prevention [[1]](/library/nPb72F)




* Lifestyle modifications  [[1]](/library/nPb72F)[[16]](/library/prYLRq)

* <u>Stress</u> reduction

* Low-<u>sodium</u> diet (1500–2300 mg per day)

* Identification and avoidance of dietary and environmental triggers (e.g., <u>caffeine</u>, <u>alcohol</u>, <u>nicotine</u>, and <u>stress</u>).

* <u>Vestibular rehabilitation</u> and <u>physical therapy</u>

* Indications: chronic imbalance , incomplete central vestibular compensation after <u>ablative therapy</u>

* Options: <u>vestibular habituation</u> exercises (e.g., <u>Cawthorne-Cooksey exercises</u>) and physical exercises that increase stability and help with balance and walking

* Other:

* <u>Allergen testing</u>, avoidance, and treatment  [[1]](/library/nPb72F)

* Patients should be educated about avoiding known triggers and the natural course of the disease, including recurrence and worsening of <u>SNHL</u> with each attack.





### <u>Maintenance therapy</u> [[1]](/library/nPb72F)




Patients with frequently recurring episodes of Meniere disease may be considered for chronic pharmacotherapy.




* <u>Diuretics</u>  [[1]](/library/nPb72F)

* <u>Thiazide diuretics</u>;  (with or without a <u>potassium-sparing diuretic</u>) are commonly used (e.g., <u>hydrochlorothiazide</u>;  DOSAGE, <u>hydrochlorothiazide</u>/<u>triamterene</u> DOSAGE).

* <u>Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor</u> (e.g., <u>acetazolamide</u> DOSAGE) [[17]](/library/m4bVPF)

* Other agents:  : systemic <u>steroids</u>, antivirals, <u>benzodiazepines</u>, betahistine  [[18]](/library/k5bm48)[[19]](/library/54biPF)

* Monitoring and duration

* Patients should be monitored frequently for:

* Symptomatic improvement

* Drug intolerance and side effects (e.g., measurement of <u>BMP</u> in patients on <u>diuretics</u>)

* Medications can be tapered off once symptoms subside.

* Duration of therapy has not been established.





### Interventional therapy [[1]](/library/nPb72F)




* Chemical <u>ablation</u> with intratympanic <u>gentamicin</u> (injection of <u>gentamicin</u> into the <u>middle ear</u> through the <u>tympanic membrane</u>) 

* First-line for patients with unilateral Meniere disease with recurrent or intractable symptoms unresponsive to pharmacological therapy

* Usually well-tolerated

* Greatly reduces <u>vertigo</u> attacks and improves <u>vertigo</u> symptoms  [[1]](/library/nPb72F)

* Intratympanic <u>steroid</u> therapy (injection of <u>methylprednisolone</u> or <u>dexamethasone</u> into the <u>middle ear</u> through the <u>tympanic membrane</u>)





> [!WARNING]
> Positive pressure <u>pulse generator</u> devices (e.g., Meniett device) are no longer recommended for Meniere disease.




### Surgical intervention [[1]](/library/nPb72F)




* Labyrinthectomy (<u>Hearing</u>-sacrificing <u>surgery</u>): destruction and removal of the labyrinth through the mastoid

* Vestibular neurectomy (<u>Hearing</u> preservation <u>surgery</u>): selective transection of the vestibular nerve within the <u>middle cranial fossa</u> via a <u>craniotomy</u>

* Endolymph drainage procedures (e.g., sacculotomy  , cochleosacculotomy , endolymph sac decompression ): No longer recommended as they are of doubtful clinical benefit  [[1]](/library/nPb72F)[[20]](/library/WNbPZ8)
